tests.description: Timed check on Key Concepts in Sociology

questions.question: Explain the difference between primary and secondary socialisation, with examples.
questions.correctAnswer: Primary socialisation: family teaches basic norms (saying please/thank you), language, right/wrong, and core values (honesty, respect). Secondary socialisation: school teaches punctuality, obedience and competition (the hidden curriculum); peers teach group norms and identity; media teaches values and consumer behaviour; religion teaches moral codes.

questions.question: Describe the relationship between norms, values and sanctions.
questions.correctAnswer: Values are broad beliefs (e.g. 'education is important'). Norms are specific rules that put values into practice (e.g. 'attend school every day', 'complete homework'). Sanctions enforce norms: positive sanctions reward conformity (praise for good work), negative sanctions punish deviance (detention for being late). questions.question: Evaluate whether socialisation determines our identity or whether we have free choice.
questions.correctAnswer: Socialisation shapes identity: gender socialisation teaches 'masculine' and 'feminine' behaviour; class socialisation teaches aspirations and tastes; ethnic socialisation teaches cultural traditions. However, individuals also have agency: they can accept, modify or reject socialised norms (e.g. choosing non-traditional gender roles). questions.question: Full-Mark Response Evaluate the importance of socialisation in shaping human behaviour. <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: A grade 9 response will: define socialisation and distinguish primary from secondary; describe key agents (family, school, peers, media) with examples of norms/values learned; argue socialisation is crucial (feral children show what happens without it); argue agency matters (people resist and reinterpret socialisation); conclude: socialisation provides the framework within which identity develops, but individuals actively construct their identity within this framework. Neither socialisation alone nor individual choice alone explains human behaviour.
